title: Robust Tool-Augmented Language Agents: Learning, Composing, and Recovering in Open-Ended API Environments
background:
Tool-augmented language agents have emerged as a dominant paradigm for extending large language models (LLMs) beyond their parametric knowledge, enabling them to invoke external APIs, execute code, and orchestrate multi-step workflows. Recent systems such as ToolFormer-style self-supervised tool induction [1] and retrieval-augmented tool selection frameworks like ToolBench-R [2] have shown that agents can learn to invoke hundreds of APIs from natural language documentation. Compositional benchmarks including AgentBoard-2025 [3] and the open-world API arena MetaTool-X [4] further demonstrate that frontier models can chain 5-10 tool calls for moderately complex tasks. In parallel, reflective and self-debugging agents [5] have improved robustness on closed tool sets through verifier-guided rollouts.

Despite this progress, three fundamental gaps persist. First, agents remain brittle when API documentation is incomplete, ambiguous, or evolves over time; recent audits show success rates collapse from 78% to under 31% under realistic documentation drift [2][4]. Second, compositional generalization beyond training distributions is poor: agents memorize call templates rather than inferring tool semantics, leading to combinatorial failures when novel tools must be composed with familiar ones [3]. Third, failure recovery in open-ended environments is largely heuristic. Existing approaches rely on fixed retry budgets or LLM-as-judge critics that themselves hallucinate, with no principled account of when to replan, decompose, or abstain [5][6]. Bridging these gaps requires new theory and systems for grounded API semantics, compositional tool reasoning, and verifiable recovery policies under partial observability.
challenges: Learning faithful, executable API semantics from heterogeneous and incomplete documentation (mixed natural language, OpenAPI specs, code examples), including handling undocumented side effects, rate limits, and authentication state
Achieving compositional generalization to unseen tool combinations without exponential demonstration data, including type-aware argument binding and cross-tool state tracking across long horizons

Designing failure-recovery policies that distinguish recoverable errors (transient, malformed arguments) from unrecoverable ones (semantic mismatch, missing capability), with calibrated abstention and minimal redundant API calls
Establishing benchmarks and evaluation protocols for open-ended tool ecosystems where the tool set evolves, ground truth is non-unique, and side effects on external systems must be sandboxed safely
Providing formal guarantees or probabilistic bounds on agent behavior (cost, latency, correctness) under adversarial or drifting API environments
